title: How to Build an Investor List That Gets You Meetings
summary: How to Build an Investor List That Gets You Meetings
body_markdown:
The easiest part of fundraising is finding investor names. Search for seed investors and you'll find enough people to keep you busy for a year. A better question is which ten would understand your company before you got to slide five.


The answer usually starts with companies, not investors. Find a few businesses that sell to the same kind of buyer but don't compete with you. Read the announcements for the rounds they raised at your stage. Then find the person who worked on the deal. The firm is a useful fact. The person is the one who has to decide whether to take a meeting.


## Ten places to look, depending on what you're missing


- [OpenVC](https://www.openvc.app/investor-lists/) . Filter reported investor profiles by how you’re raising. Confirm claims against the firm site.
- [NFX Signal](https://signal.nfx.com/) . Look for individual investors with relevant stage or sector. Confirm current firm and role.
- [NVCA Members](https://nvca.org/nvca-members/) . Identify firms in the U.S. venture ecosystem. Membership does not establish fit or activity.
- [Angel Capital Association Directory](https://angelcapitalassociation.org/directory/) . Find organized groups and navigate to an official submission page. Verify each group’s geography and criteria.
- [Gust investor search](https://gust.com/search/new?accepting_applications=true&category=investors) . Find groups that publicly list applications. Confirm status directly with the group.
- [YC Startup Directory](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies) . Work backward from useful comparisons and their round announcements. Directory entry is not investor evidence.
- [Techstars Portfolio](https://www.techstars.com/portfolio) . Search for companies close to your buyer or problem. Verify investor facts in company announcements.
- [SBA SBIC Directory](https://legacy.sba.gov/funding-programs/investment-capital/sbic-directory) . Find relevant licensed fund managers before checking mandate. Not a default route for a generic pre-seed round.
- [SEC EDGAR Search](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings) . Find public filings, including available Form D notices. A filing does not establish investor interest or disclose every participant.
- [SEC Investment Adviser Public Disclosure](https://adviserinfo.sec.gov/) . Look up records for advisers available in the database. Not a complete list of investors and not an endorsement.


## Make every row earn its place


For each prospect, write down a piece of evidence and the sentence you'd use to explain why you're reaching out. If you can only write “invests in software,” skip them for now. “You backed an early product that first sold to independent clinics” is more useful. It tells you what to say and what you expect the investor to understand.


Keep discovery and qualification separate. A database profile is a good way to find a name. A recent deal announcement, partner bio, or public investing thesis is a better reason to move that name up the list. Keep the source URL and date in the row. Someone's role changes; the last time you checked is a useful fact.


## Get better at guessing before you send more


Try a first batch of ten. Choose people for whom you have evidence, use the right public route or a real introduction, and keep the notes short. Look at the replies. “We only invest after revenue” tells you something about your list. “I don't understand who buys this” tells you something about your pitch. If both notes say the same thing, revise before sending the next ten.


A useful sheet has six working columns: investor, person, comparable deal, why they fit, public route, and next step. Add a last-checked date. When you can explain every name in the first batch, you have enough to start.
